title: Dhurandhar Just Crossed ₹3,100 Crore. Now It's Coming for Japan.
excerpt: Ranveer Singh recorded a personal video for Japanese audiences. On July 10, the biggest Hindi franchise in history opens in one of Asia's toughest cinema markets.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dhurandhar franchise grossed over ₹3,100 crore, redefining Bollywood's global potential.
  • Dhurandhar: The Revenge is the first Hindi film to surpass ₹1,000 crore net in India.
  • Ranveer Singh's personal outreach targets Japanese audiences for the franchise's Japan debut.
  • The film's release in Japan marks a strategic push into a challenging market for Indian cinema.
  • Dhurandhar's success signals a shift in Bollywood's global distribution strategy.

Somewhere in a recording studio, Ranveer Singh looked into a camera and spoke directly to Japanese audiences. Not in Hindi. Not through a translator. In a carefully crafted video message designed to feel personal, inviting a country that has never been a traditional market for Bollywood to experience the most dominant Indian franchise of the decade on the big screen.

Dhurandhar: The Revenge opens in Japan on July 10, and the significance of that date extends well beyond a new territory getting showtimes. This is a statement film arriving in a market that has historically treated Indian cinema as a curiosity — and it's arriving not as an experiment, but as a conqueror. The combined worldwide gross of the Dhurandhar franchise has now crossed ₹3,100 crore. That number doesn't just lead Bollywood. It rewrites the conversation about what Hindi-language cinema can achieve globally.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=o7Z9MIkddZM

The Numbers Behind the Swagger

Director Aditya Dhar's two-film franchise has achieved something that seemed mathematically impossible even two years ago. The sequel alone — *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* — stands at over ₹1,813 crore worldwide. More importantly, it became the first purely Hindi-language film to breach the ₹1,000 crore net mark in India. Not a multi-language release. Not a dubbed South Indian blockbuster crossing linguistic borders. A Hindi film, made for Hindi audiences, that simply refused to stop collecting.

The first installment laid the groundwork. The sequel detonated it. Together, they've built the kind of franchise muscle that Bollywood has dreamed about since the *Baahubali* films proved Indian cinema could play in the same arena as Hollywood tentpoles.

> "The sequel alone — *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* — stands at over ₹1,813 crore worldwide."

Why Japan Matters

Japan is not an obvious market for Indian movies. It's a country with deeply entrenched local cinema traditions, an appetite for anime and Hollywood blockbusters, and a moviegoing culture that doesn't naturally gravitate toward South Asian storytelling. But something has been shifting.

Recent years have seen Japanese audiences develop a genuine appetite for large-scale Indian action films with high production values. The visual ambition, the practical stunts, the unrestrained emotional intensity — these elements resonate in a market that appreciates craft and spectacle. Jio Studios is betting that Dhurandhar's particular brand of geopolitical thriller — Ranveer's undercover agent Hamza Ali Mazari navigating a high-stakes espionage narrative — has the right blend of kinetic action and narrative tension to cross that cultural bridge.

The personalised video from Ranveer is a small but telling detail. Studios don't invest in market-specific outreach unless they see real potential. This isn't a quiet digital release or a limited festival screening. This is a calculated theatrical push into one of Asia's most competitive cinema markets.

What It Means for Diaspora Audiences

For the Indian diaspora — particularly the growing NRI community in Japan, estimated at over 40,000 — this release carries an emotional charge that goes beyond box office arithmetic. Watching a Hindi blockbuster on a Japanese big screen, in a country where you might go months without hearing your mother tongue at a cinema, is a different kind of experience entirely.

Bollywood's Global Strategy Shift
›Dhurandhar targets Japan as a key market.
›Strategic marketing for each international release.
›Focus on high production values and storytelling.
›Expansion rumors into South Korea and Latin America.

But the story is bigger than Japan alone. Dhurandhar's global playbook — which has already conquered North America, the UK, the Gulf, Australia, and now East Asia — represents a fundamental shift in how Bollywood distributes its biggest films. The old model was simple: release domestically, collect whatever the overseas diaspora delivers, and move on. The new model, the one Aditya Dhar and Jio Studios are building, treats every major international market as a first-class release territory with its own strategy, its own marketing, its own star outreach.

The Aditya Dhar Effect

It's worth pausing on the director. Aditya Dhar has, in the span of two films, built the most commercially dominant franchise in Hindi cinema history. Not through spectacle alone — though the Dhurandhar films deliver that in abundance — but through a combination of tight geopolitical storytelling, a lead performance from Ranveer that has silenced every critic who questioned his range, and a visual scale that holds up against anything coming out of Hollywood's action pipeline.

The franchise's ₹3,100 crore combined gross puts it in territory that only a handful of Indian film series have ever approached. And unlike some of those, Dhurandhar achieved it without the multi-language release strategy that typically inflates all-India numbers. This is a Hindi franchise that earns like a pan-India event.

What Comes Next

With the Japan release, the Dhurandhar franchise is signalling that its global ambitions are far from satisfied. Rumours of further expansion into South Korea and Latin America have circulated in trade circles, though nothing has been confirmed. What's clear is that Ranveer Singh — already the single biggest box-office earner of 2026's first half — now has a franchise that functions like a global brand, not just a film series.

For Japanese audiences walking into theatres on July 10, they'll see what Indian audiences already know: a spy thriller that moves like a bullet train, looks like it cost three times what it did, and features a leading man operating at the absolute peak of his powers. If that doesn't translate across borders, nothing will.
